newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition protests as tensions run high.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition protests as tensions run high.

text.p: Serbia's opposition kept up an unprecedented wave of protests on Thursday as President Slobodan Milosevic's Socialist government cracked down on independent media.

Vuk Draskovic, a flamboyant writer and a leader of the opposition Zajedno coalition, appealed for calm to avoid a repetition of Tuesday's scenes when protesters smashed plate glass windows state television and newspaper offices.

A 700-metre long column of opposition supporters, which appeared larger than the previous day's when 80,000 took to the streets, again pelted the buildings with eggs and firecrackers but the damage was limited to egg stains.
Zajedno has led more than a week of demonstrations since the authorities annulled results of municipal polls which handed unexpected victories to the opposition.
The opposition said it won 15 of Serbia's 18 largest towns including Belgrade, but electoral commissions overturned the results in most towns for unspecified "irregularities".
Belgrade residents leaned from their apartments along the route of Wednesday's march, making a Serbian three-fingered salute and cheering Draskovic and his supporters.
Asked why Wednesday's march took a different route from previous demonstrations, Draskovic said: "We will keep changing our path and reclaim the city street by street."
Activists urged the jeering marchers not to linger in front of a cordon of riot police, hoping to avoid clashes.
Before television cameras, Draskovic pulled a tram driver who rang his bell to support the marchers from his cab and embraced him.
"I welcome you to our ranks, and I hope all your colleagues will follow your lead," he said.
Another opposition leader, Zoran Djindjic, said trades union support was vital to the success of the anti-Milosevic campaign.

The Association of Independent Trade Unions, which says it represents 700,000 workers, issued a call to its members to join the protest. Chairman Dragan Milovanovac said it was possible a strike would be called from Monday.

"The regime is very afraid of workers," he told Reuters. "It is the old communist conviction that when workers go out on the streets it is the end and they are now trying in every possible way (to prevent that)."

The capital's only independent radio station, B-92, said its signal was jammed every time it attempted to broadcast news. Journalists walked out of another newspaper complaining of editorial censorship under pressure from the authorities.
Milosevic brutually crushed similar protests in 1991 with tanks and water cannon. This time he faces demonstrations in several other towns across the country.
Large numbers of workers have joined rallies in Kragujevac and Nis, industrial towns that were once Milosevic strongholds.

Re-run elections took place on Wednesday in cities where results 10 days ago were overturned. The opposition urged a boycott in Belgrade, but state media reported the Socialists had secured enough seats to form a majority.
